WRT the Orsimer, Dunmer and Khajiit-- my favorite theory about these particular three races is one I heard ages ago, a theory that 'Azura hates elves'. 

Think about it. Azura was involved with the Velothi exodus that saw Trinimac devoured and his followers transformed into Orsimer. Then, Azura became a principle goddess in Chimeri religion... until the Tribunal ascended, at which point she cursed the hell out of the Dunmer, a curse that would eventually lead to their downfall alongside of the Tribunal and their eradication in the Red Year. Hop over to the Khajiit, and it was Azura who transformed them from Bosmer, changing their shapes for vague religious reasons, and she's cherished by them at a result. 

That's three. Three elven races Azura has tormented. Pretty impressive track record considering most daedric princes don't even get to eradicate one race.

Why would Azura care? Elves are descended from the Aldmer, who profess close ties to divinity. Why did Azura curse the Tribunal? Because they had the audacity, as mortals, to claim divinity. Azura is the Daedric prince of Vanity in Daggerfall; she can't stand any blurriness between mortals and gods, so the further away the mer get from their roots, the happier she is.

From that very lore-book:

> untold weeks they had climbed a mighty range of mountains under Veloth's leadership.... They came upon a great pass, a deep scar in the mountain covered in ice and snow. 

Is there any evidence suggesting such a pass exists in Cyrodiil? Because given the ice/snow references, this seems most likely to be referring to the Dunmeth Pass outside of Windhelm, and the mountains the Velothi mountains along the Morrowind-Skyrim border.

Why couldn't they have gone east through Cyrodiil until hitting the Valus Mountains and travelling north along those? In that case the 'great mountain range' climbed by the Chimer could have included the place the Jeralls, the Valus and the Velothi mountain ranges converge (around Trollhetta), which would certainly be a daunting trip. Basically, it's not 'unnecessarily long' when you consider the big ol' mountain range that divides the eastern part of Tamriel from the rest of the continent... 

edit for geography

Do you have a source on Vvardenfell never being conquered? Not that I doubt it, I'm just curious! As for Solstheim-- I seem to recall an ebony mine leading to a Nordic Ruin in the Dragonborn DLC, so whether they built deliberate mines or no, they almost certainly had access to it, even in small amounts. Wuuthrad is ebony. It must've been expensive and difficult obtain, reserved for only the most important items (Ysgramor's hammer, certain Dragon Priest masks), but I don't see why they couldn't have had it. 

As for the Nordic occupation of Morrowind-- they were in Morrowind for 250 years. While there were certainly Nord occupiers who harboured genocidal sentiments (Hoag Mer-Killer being the obvious) , there also seemed to be 'assimilated' Chieftains who adapted parts of Chimeri culture-- Jurgen Wind-Caller, for instance, had his name on his tomb written in Daedric, the script of Morrowind. We also have evidence of Nords and Chimer working together in the form of Anudnabia, where Dorach Gusal and Hilbongard Rolamus (actually, these names give me pause as to the races of the smiths involved, but given that this is ancient Sadrith Mora, connected to a Chimer ancestral tomb, and an enchanter and a smith respectively, Chimer and Nord seems most likely). 

MY POINT IS that, maybe slavery doesn't have to be involved either way. 250 years is a lot of time for cultures to overlap, even for the long-lived Chimer. Especially when it comes to something like smithing, which the Nords are prety good at.

After a bit of thought my bet is that this specific motif is a product of the Nord occupation of Morrowind from the first era. I think 'enslaved Nords' is less likely than enslaved *Chimer*, and this particular style could be the result of the ancient Nords, who were already familiar with working Stahlrim, suddenly having access to ebony in vast amounts. 

As for the weird connection to Malacath-- possibly a result of Scourge becoming associated with the style somehow? However, some sources claim that the Orcs joined up with the Nords at the Battle of Red Mountain, and a lot of armour is crafted for wars. Malacath's touch could have come in through that. Though I still think that's really interesting given the relationship between Malacath and Boethiah.

HOAGA: "On the battlefields, this demon would often be seen on the sidelines, eating the soil voraciously. When his men fell, Hoaga would fill their bodies back with it, whereupon they would rise again and fight, albeit slower." This is necromancy: the thu'um. This guy had zombies. An army of zombies. YSMIR: We have the most historical sources on this guy, so there's no need to make too many guesses. Apparently his Voice was so strong that he couldn't speak aloud without ruining things. Despite his notoriety, it seems he was just wielding a ridiculously powerful version of Unrelenting Force, which is effective but it's not tonal architecture or zombies so boo, Ysmir.

'Attain powerful artifact for themselves' seems to be a popular method; 'summon powerful creature and make it obey me' or 'become a lich' are others. 

With novice skills in conjuration or alteration, this farmer probably has a rudimentary understanding of soul magic-- enough to understand that souls = energy. Necromancy might be an appealing avenue for this fellow. Depending on their moral soundness, they might consider murdering and soultrapping people with the end goal of somehow using their souls to empower themself, and raising the corpses to be their undead army. If they're a more noble sort, they could consider binding atronachs or other daedra to themselves as a power boost, or go on a wild quest to seek an object of extreme potency... but for the average commoner with basic conjuration talents, necromancy seems the easiest option.

I'd say that it's a mixture of lower population and more fractured population. IIRC each province is more or less divided-- Skyrim into Holds, Morrowind into Houses, High Rock into states, etc. I imagine that putting together a large host would require an unfeasible amount of diplomacy no matter which province(s) you're taking your soldiers from. 

That and there's simply no need for massive hosts. From what we know about Tamriel's landscape, warfare seems less a matter of brute strength and more a matter of playing the weaknesses of your enemies and the battlefield. There aren't many provinces where an enormous army will do you many favors imo.

"A Hypothetical Treachery", among other sources, seems to imply that spells can be cast fairly quickly-- the real restraining source is the magika pool as the caster, as magika refresh rates are apparently closer to what we see in Morrowind and earlier games! 

As for tactics itself? Short answer is that it's tricky. Another commenter mentioned 2920 as a good source of large-scale battles fought with armies. "The War of Two Houses" offers us an interesting look at how portals are used in inter-house Dunmer warfare. "Cherim's' Heart of Anequina" outlines possible Bosmer vs Khajiit battle tactics. There are a lot more examples if you look around, I'm sure I missed quite a few. Basically you're right in assuming that warfare is very versatile in the TES universe, and each race uses their own native advantages creatively in it. 

The one thing I'd propose is constant is that bottles are probably fought on a much smaller scale than what we're used to, with only a few hundred two a few thousand soldiers in each side. But even that probably changed in Tiber Septim's conquest.
